summary: R. Meir explicitly rules the HP's bull is a communal sin-offering (supporting Abaye): it cannot become pigul and overrides Shabbat/tumah. R. Elazar then raises and resolves his dilemma: the Yom Kippur service is exclusively designated (yuchad) - the HP cannot simultaneously fulfill personal votive obligations through it, regardless of whether the bull is classified as communal or personal.

learning.ahaMoment: R. Meir's communal ruling is the clearest tannaitic statement: the HP represents all Israel, so his bull is communal.
learning.memoryAnchor: R. Meir: HP's bull = communal offering. 'For himself and his household' describes his role, not a limitation.
learning.learnerQuestion: What does R. Meir's explicit ruling on the status of the High Priest's bull settle, and how does it bear on the Abaye-Rava dispute?
learning.coreTension: The HP brings a bull described as 'for himself and his household,' but R. Meir rules it is in fact a communal sin-offering (chatat tzibur), creating tension with any reading that limits the bull's scope to the HP's personal or household atoning function.
learning.coreMove: R. Meir's explicit ruling that the HP's bull is a communal chatat anchors the Abaye-Rava dispute in tannaitic tradition, showing that the communal reading is not Abaye's invention but reflects a tanna's direct ruling that the HP's role encompasses all Israel.

takeaway.text: R. Meir rules explicitly that the High Priest's Yom Kippur bull is a communal sin-offering (chatat tzibur), establishing the communal-representative reading as a tannaitic position - not merely an amoraic inference.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may think the communal interpretation of the HP's bull is Abaye's creative reading with no tannaitic foundation, missing that R. Meir's explicit ruling provides direct tannaitic support for the communal-offering status.

learning.ahaMoment: The Yom Kippur service is not just important - it is legally exclusive. No personal obligation can be grafted onto it.
learning.memoryAnchor: HP on Yom Kippur: his entire service is designated for national atonement. No personal obligation may share that designation.
learning.learnerQuestion: Can the High Priest use the Yom Kippur service to simultaneously fulfill a personal votive obligation?
learning.coreTension: The HP performs the Yom Kippur service as the national representative, but if he personally holds a vow that his designated offering could also discharge, the question is whether the Yom Kippur service is exclusive to its designated purpose or can serve both functions at once.
learning.coreMove: R. Elazar rules the Yom Kippur service is exclusively designated (yuchad) for its own purpose, prohibiting the HP from using it to also discharge a personal vow - the service belongs to the day and its atoning function, not to any personal obligation of the HP.

takeaway.text: R. Elazar rules the Yom Kippur service is exclusively designated (yuchad) for its own purpose - the High Priest may not simultaneously use it to discharge a personal votive obligation.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume the HP can direct the service toward dual purposes since he is performing the act anyway, missing R. Elazar's ruling that the exclusivity of the service prohibits any co-opting for personal obligations.

rashiTranslations.en: According to the one who says, etc. - Rabbi Meir called it above an individual offering. What
is his question - for it is certainly obvious to us that his fellow priests achieve atonement through it
and a partnership offering does not generate a substitute - so what is his uncertainty about it? New comment: 'if we say'
'if we follow the one who consecrated it' - regarding substitution, and this is an individual who consecrated it from his own property,
it comes, and not from partnership property. New comment: 'or if we follow'
'the one who achieves atonement' - and many achieve atonement
through it. New comment: 'obviously' - for regarding substitution, the one who achieves atonement
is its owner - as Rabbi Abahu said in the name of Rabbi
Yochanan: three things apply to one who gives from his own property
to discharge another's obligation. New comment: 'the one who consecrates' - his animal,
so that another can fulfill through it an obligation upon him - the one who consecrates
is the owner regarding the added fifth, if
it became blemished and he comes to redeem it; but if
the one who achieves atonement comes to redeem it, he does not need to add
the fifth, since regarding the fifth it is written (Leviticus 27):
'and if the one who consecrated shall redeem it, etc.' - the one who consecrated, and not
the one who achieves atonement. New comment: 'and the one who achieves atonement performs substitution with it' -
but if the one who consecrated performs substitution with it, it is not
a valid substitution, since one cannot exchange another's property, and this
is not his own property. New comment: 'and one who tithes from his own produce' -
on behalf of another - the benefit is his. It is in his power
to give it to whichever priest he wishes; and if another comes
and says, 'here is this sela, and give this terumah to the son of
my daughter, a priest' - it is his, for the terumah is his to designate,
as it is stated: 'when you have finished tithing all
the tithe of your produce, etc., and you shall give it to the Levite, etc.'
(Deuteronomy 26) - the verse makes the giving dependent on the one
whose tithe it is, from his own produce. New comment: 'do they achieve atonement fixedly' -
like other cases of achieving atonement where others set aside the animal
on their behalf, who transferred ownership of the animal to them for atonement,
so too here, a portion in it is acquired by them, and it becomes
a partnership sin-offering with respect to substitution. New comment: 'or
perhaps they achieve atonement only floatingly' - meaning, their
atonement is not fixed through it, but rather floats on top of
the High Priest's atonement, like something that floats on the surface of
the water, and the offering is not called by their name,
and it is an individual offering. Proof-text: 'and the iron floated' (II Kings 6)
is rendered in Targum as 'ukfa parzela', it floated. New comment: 'a stringency in the sacrifice' -
since it comes as the initial consecration, greater than the substitute which was exchanged
onto it. New comment: 'that the sacrifice, etc.' - it will explain further on
and go, in which sacrifice you find this. New comment: 'which is not'
'so in the substitute' - for the substitute does not apply to the community,
and does not override Shabbat, since it has no fixed time,
and does not generate a substitute, as it is written, 'and it and
its substitute shall be' - and not the substitute of a substitute.
'that the substitute takes effect' - inherent sanctity comes upon it,
even if it has a permanent blemish at the time of substitution, and if one comes to redeem it, it does not
go out to non-sacred use except regarding slaughter and eating alone, but not to be shorn or worked, for there is no
distinction in it between unblemished and blemished, as it is written (Leviticus 27): 'bad for good, or good for bad,
and if he shall indeed exchange it, etc.' New comment: 'unlike the sacrifice' - for if the sacrifice's consecration preceded
its blemish, it does not go out through its redemption to non-sacred use to be shorn or worked, as it is written regarding disqualified consecrated animals
(Deuteronomy 12): 'you shall slaughter and eat meat' - you may slaughter it, but not its wool, and not its milk; but
if its blemish preceded its consecration, it is like one who consecrates wood and stones for the value of a burnt-offering, which has no
inherent sanctity upon them, only monetary sanctity, and they go out through their redemption to non-sacred use
completely, as we learned in Tractate Bechorot (14a) and in the laws of slaughtering non-sacred animals (Chullin 130a). New comment: 'rather, must it not
be referring to the bull' - of Yom Kippur, which applies to the community as to an individual, since it is a sin-offering, and a sin-offering
applies to the community and generates a substitute - so this shows that the Yom Kippur bull generates a substitute.
'referring to Aharon's ram' - of Yom Kippur. New comment: 'what is meant by substitute - the name substitute' - actually
referring to the bull, and this stringency in the sacrifice over the substitute that is taught does not refer to its own substitute,
rather it means this: a stringency in the sacrifice over the NAME substitute - for you have nothing whose name is
'substitute' that overrides Shabbat, even substitutes that are otherwise sacrificable. New comment: 'if so' - since it teaches the NAME
'sacrifice' too, let it teach the NAME 'sacrifice' - and since the Tanna would then be teaching the name 'sacrifice,' why are you forced to establish it
as referring to one single sacrifice, from which you would derive that it speaks of Aharon's bull or of his ram? Perhaps
the Tanna means this: a stringency in the thing called 'sacrifice' over the thing called 'substitute,' for there is
a sacrifice that applies to the community as to an individual, and there is a sacrifice that overrides Shabbat, such as

communal or individual, whose time is fixed; and there is a sacrifice that generates a substitute, such as an individual offering. New comment: 'it does not teach the name sacrifice' - this Tanna, rather, phrased his statement using one sacrifice as an example.
A firstborn animal (continues on 51a).
